---
title: "Centaur or cyborg: what you hand to the machine, and what you keep"
subtitle: "AIM-5 · AIM-X · AIM-4 · about one hour"
---

::: {.callout-note title="What you'll learn"}
By the end of this chapter you will have:

1. Used a chatbot for three everyday tasks of a new intern, and kept the
   prompt that worked best as something you will use again.
2. Decided, for a task, whether to work with the machine as a centaur or a
   cyborg, by asking what happens if the output is wrong.
3. Turned a prompt that asks for an answer into one that asks for a hint, and
   had the tool quiz you.
4. Named the three ways a tool can cost you a skill, and the habit that
   protects against each.
5. Written down the one part of clinical judgment you will not hand over, and
   why.
:::

**Time.** About 20 minutes of reading, 45 minutes of doing, and five minutes
at the end. The podcast is optional. Use your university ChatGPT Edu or
Microsoft Copilot account; any free chatbot also works. There is nothing to
install.

## The first list

It is 6:10 on the first Monday of intern year. You have six patients, a
badge that opens more doors than it should, and a list.

```{=html}
<div style="max-width:520px;margin:1.2em auto;padding:1em 1.3em;background:#fffdf5;color:#1f2328;border:1px solid #e0d9c3;border-left:6px solid #c9a227;font-family:'Segoe UI',Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif;box-shadow:2px 2px 0 #e0d9c3;">
<div style="font-size:.75em;letter-spacing:.1em;text-transform:uppercase;color:#7a6a3a;">Mon · day 1 · before rounds</div>
<ol style="margin:.5em 0 .3em 1.2em;padding:0;line-height:1.55;">
<li>Pre-round: beds 4, 7, 9, 12, 14, 15. Overnight events, vitals, labs.</li>
<li>Progress notes x6 before 8:00.</li>
<li>Discharge summary, bed 12 (admitted 11 days ago; three services involved).</li>
<li>Portal inbox: four patient messages from the weekend.</li>
<li>Call nephrology about bed 9. What exactly are we asking?</li>
<li>Journal club slides, Thursday. Have not picked the paper.</li>
</ol>
<div style="font-size:.7em;color:#8a7a5a;border-top:1px solid #e0d9c3;padding-top:.4em;margin-top:.4em;">Illustrative intern task list, made up for this chapter. No patient on it is real.</div>
</div>
```

Your senior resident has been an intern for exactly one year. She looks at the
list and says what every senior says now: "Have it draft the notes. Have it
draft the discharge summary. That's what it's for." She is right that it can.
She has also found uses nobody told her about. She gets the gist of a paper in
five minutes. She rewrites patient handouts so a twelve-year-old could follow
them. She rehearses phone calls she is dreading.

So look at the list again with two questions. For each line, what could the
machine do for you that you have not thought of? And if you hand it over, what
do you get back, and what do you lose? The notes are the easy case. Even there
the answer splits in two. A note that is *drafted* for you and a note that is
*written* by you are different things that share one template. The discharge
summary is harder. It is the only document on the list that forces you to read
eleven days of chart and decide what happened to this person. The consult
question is a different kind of hard. The machine will produce a very good
question. But the reason you are calling is that you do not yet know what to
ask.

This chapter is about that sorting, and about getting good at the part you do
hand over. **It is your job to learn where these tools help your work.** Nobody
can do the sorting for you, and the way to learn it is to try.

If you would rather try first and read after, open your chatbot now and do
task 1 of the [Do](#do). Then come back.

## Why this matters

In three months, the list above is yours, and the tool will be in the chart
whether or not you have decided how to use it. Two of this course's faculty,
speaking in last year's course, describe the two ends of this. One asked
whether avoiding AI is really an option (Chad Stickrath, MD). The other, a
pediatric hospitalist, said we should be scared, because what we do is scary
(Christina Olson, MD). Both are right. This chapter is about using the tool,
and using it well, while keeping the second in mind.

There is one thing specific to your stage of training. You are about to learn
clinical reasoning on real patients, with a tool that produces a plausible
answer to every question you were supposed to struggle with. Used one way, it
makes you better faster. Used another way, it stops you learning. The
difference is mostly in how you ask.

## How it works

### Two ways to work with a machine

Start with a randomized trial and a puzzle. [The appraisal
chapter](core-appraisal.qmd), in week 2, comes back to it. Fifty physicians were each given six
diagnostic cases. Half also had a language model: the kind of AI behind
ChatGPT and Copilot. The physicians with the model did no better than the
physicians without it. The adjusted difference was 2 points on a 100-point
reasoning score (95% CI −4 to 8). The model working alone scored 16 points
above the physicians (95% CI 2 to 30) [@pmid:39466245].

::: {#fig-goh}


Median diagnostic-reasoning score per case, as a percentage of the rubric, in
the 2024 randomized trial. The model-alone bar is drawn at 74 + 16, because the
paper reports the difference, not a median. Redrawn from the published numbers
[@pmid:39466245]; data are not copyrightable.
:::

The tool was capable. The physicians did not get the benefit. The same group
ran a second trial a year later, on management rather than diagnosis. This
time the physicians with the model scored 6.5 points higher than those without
(95% CI 2.7 to 10.2), and could not be told apart from the model alone
[@pmid:39910272]. Same team, same kind of tool, opposite result. What changed
was the task, and how the physicians worked with it. That is a skill, and
skills can be learned.

There are names for the ways of working. They come from a 2023 experiment in
which several hundred management consultants were given GPT-4, and researchers
watched how the successful ones worked [@doi:10.2139/ssrn.4573321]:

- A **centaur** divides the work. There is a clean line between the human half
  and the horse half. You give the machine one clearly marked piece of the
  task, keep the rest, and check what comes back before you use it.
- A **cyborg** blends the work. You move back and forth with the machine
  inside a single piece of work: drafting a sentence, asking for three
  alternatives, taking one, rewriting it, asking what is missing.

The same study found something worth remembering. The tool helped most on
tasks inside what it could do well, and hurt on tasks just outside it. The
authors called that uneven edge the **jagged frontier**. You cannot see where
the frontier runs from the outside. You find it by trying things.

Neither way of working is the correct one. The skill is knowing which a task
calls for. The 2025 *NEJM* review this chapter is based on gives a simple rule
[@pmid:40834302]: work as a centaur when the stakes are high or the tool is
not validated for that use; work as a cyborg when the task is low-risk or
creative. @fig-modes turns that into two questions.

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-modes
%%| fig-alt: "Decision flowchart. The task in front of you leads to the question, if the output is wrong, who is harmed and how badly. If a patient, seriously, ask whether any tool is validated for this exact use at your institution. No leads to centaur or not at all, hand over one clear piece and check every line. Yes leads to centaur, hand over the one piece and check before signing. If mostly me or nobody, ask whether the tool is validated for this use. No leads to cyborg is reasonable, stay involved and check what matters. Yes leads to cyborg, go back and forth freely."
%%| fig-cap: "Which way of working a task calls for. Two questions to ask before you open the tool. Adapted from the framework in Abdulnour et al. (2025)."
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Which way of working a task calls for
  accDescr: Decision flowchart. The task in front of you leads to the question, if the output is wrong, who is harmed and how badly. If a patient, seriously, ask whether any tool is validated for this exact use at your institution. No leads to centaur or not at all, hand over one clear piece and check every line. Yes leads to centaur, hand over the one piece and check before signing. If mostly me or nobody, ask whether the tool is validated for this use. No leads to cyborg is reasonable, stay involved and check what matters. Yes leads to cyborg, go back and forth freely.
  T["The task in front of you"] --> R{"If the output is wrong,<br/>who is harmed, and how badly?"}
  R -- "A patient, seriously" --> V1{"Is any tool validated<br/>for this exact use,<br/>at your institution?"}
  R -- "Mostly me, or nobody" --> V2{"Is the tool validated<br/>for this use?"}
  V1 -- No --> C1["Centaur, or not at all.<br/>Hand over one clear piece.<br/>Check every line."]
  V1 -- Yes --> C2["Centaur.<br/>Hand over the one piece.<br/>Check before signing."]
  V2 -- No --> C3["Cyborg is reasonable.<br/>Stay involved.<br/>Check what matters."]
  V2 -- Yes --> C4["Cyborg.<br/>Go back and forth freely."]
```

"Validated for this use" means someone has measured how the tool performs on
*this* task, on patients like yours. An ambient scribe (the tool that listens
to a visit and drafts the note), with randomized trials
behind it, is validated for drafting a visit note. The same product is not
validated for writing your discharge summary. The chatbot in the other tab is
validated for nothing on your list, which is why it belongs on the cyborg side
for low-risk work and the centaur side for anything that reaches a patient.

### Three ways to lose a skill, and how to keep it

The review names three ways a tool can cost you a skill
[@pmid:40834302]. They are worth knowing as three words, because the habit
that protects you is different for each:

- **Deskilling**: losing a skill you had. At four endoscopy centers, doctors
  found adenomas in 28.4% of colonoscopies before an AI tool arrived. A few
  months after it arrived, on days they worked without it, they found them in
  22.4%. The study is observational [@pmid:40816301].
- **Never-skilling**: never building a skill, because the tool answered
  first. In a randomized trial of nearly a thousand high-school math students,
  a plain chatbot
  raised practice scores and then *lowered* exam scores once it was taken
  away. A version set up to give hints instead of answers had a much smaller
  cost [@pmid:40560616].
- **Mis-skilling**: learning a wrong pattern from plausible output. There is
  no trial of this yet, so here is an example. Read the plan in this made-up
  draft note.

```{=html}
<div style="max-width:600px;margin:1.2em auto;padding:0;border:1px solid #cfd6df;border-radius:6px;font-family:Menlo,Consolas,'Courier New',monospace;font-size:.82em;background:#f8fafc;color:#1f2328;box-shadow:0 4px 12px rgba(0,0,0,.12);">
<div style="background:#1565c0;color:#fff;padding:.45em .9em;font-family:'Segoe UI',Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif;font-size:.9em;display:flex;justify-content:space-between;"><span>&#10024; Draft progress note &middot; hospital day 3</span><span style="opacity:.8">Accept &middot; Edit &middot; Discard</span></div>
<div style="padding:.8em 1em;line-height:1.5;color:#222;white-space:pre-wrap;">S: Pt reports breathing "a little better." Slept flat x2 pillows. No CP.
O: T 37.1 HR 88 BP 118/70 RR 18 SpO2 94% RA. Wt 84.2 kg (admit 87.0).
   JVP 8 cm. Bibasilar crackles, improved. 1+ pedal edema.
   Na 133 K 3.4 Cr 1.6 (baseline 1.0; yesterday 1.3) BUN 41.
   BNP trending down. CXR: improving vascular congestion.
A/P:
1. Acute decompensated HFrEF, improving. Continue furosemide 80 mg IV BID.
   Daily weights, strict I/O. Goal net negative 1-1.5 L.
<span style="background:#fff4cc;display:block;margin:0 -1em;padding:0 1em;">2. AKI, likely prerenal in setting of poor PO intake and diuresis.
   Continue IV fluids at 75 mL/h. Trend Cr. Hold nephrotoxins.</span>
3. Hypokalemia. Replete K to &gt;4.0.
4. HTN. Continue home lisinopril.
Dispo: continue inpatient diuresis.</div>
<div style="padding:.4em 1em;border-top:1px solid #cfd6df;font-family:'Segoe UI',Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif;font-size:.85em;color:#5a6a7a;">Illustrative draft, made up for this chapter, for a fictional patient. Not the output of any real product.</div>
</div>
```

Problem 2 is fluent and correctly formatted, and it contradicts problem 1:
it gives fluid to a patient the plan is drying out. A rising creatinine on day
3 of diuresis is the expected cost of getting fluid off. The decision an intern
should make here (hold, slow, or continue the diuretic) was made by template.
Accept that on ten patients and you have learned a pattern: creatinine up, add
fluids.

| Peril | What it is | The intern task most exposed | The defense |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Deskilling** | A skill you had fades when you stop using it | Reading your own images, ECGs, and strips before the machine's read | Do it first, then look. Keep a count of where you disagreed and who was right. |
| **Never-skilling** | A skill you never build because the tool answered first | The differential; the consult question; the discharge summary's narrative | Start on your own. Ask for hints. Take the tool away before the test, because residency will. |
| **Mis-skilling** | A wrong pattern learned from plausible output | Any drafted assessment and plan | Read the reasoning, not the conclusion. Ask *why this and not that*. Never accept a plan you could not have written. |

: Three perils, three defenses. The middle row is where a fourth-year is most exposed. {#tbl-perils}

The middle row is the one to watch as a fourth-year, and the fix is
encouraging: it is in how you ask. In a randomized study of learners, students
who worked with a chatbot did better on the task in front of them but did not
learn more. The authors' name for the behavior behind that gap is
*metacognitive laziness*: letting the tool check your thinking for you
[@doi:10.1111/bjet.13544]. Their answer to "should learners use these tools?"
is *probably, yes*. Last year's course turned their recommendations into five
habits and added a sixth:

1. **Start on your own.** Build your differential before you ask anything.
   Ask for help when you are stuck, not when you are merely unsure.
2. **Ask for hints, not answers.** Not "give me the differential." Instead:
   "I think this is cardiac and I may be missing something in the abdomen.
   What categories have I not named?"
3. **Teach back.** Explain your reasoning and ask whether it is right.
4. **Ask why.** Why this drug and not that one, why this cutoff. The reason is
   what transfers to the next patient.
5. **Use it after, too.** Once you have solved a problem yourself, ask for a
   better approach, or for what an expert would have done differently.
6. **Ask it to quiz you.** When the tool tests you, it is least able to make
   you dependent on it.

### Who, where, what

Half of the difference between a hint and an answer is in the prompt. The
pattern this course uses has three parts:

- **Who** you are: "I am a fourth-year medical student."
- **Where** you are: "I am on an inpatient medicine rotation, day 3 of a
  patient admitted with a heart-failure exacerbation."
- **What** you want, as the thing you want to *understand* rather than the
  thing you want *produced*: "I want to understand how to think about a
  rising creatinine during diuresis. Ask me what I think first."

Here is the same request both ways, for the made-up patient above.

::: {.callout-note title="Answer-seeking"}
> 67M with HFrEF exacerbation, day 3 of IV furosemide, creatinine 1.0 → 1.3 →
> 1.6. What should I do about the AKI?
:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Hint-seeking"}
> I am a fourth-year medical student on an inpatient medicine rotation. My
> patient was admitted three days ago with a heart-failure exacerbation and is
> being diuresed; weight is down 3 kg, still has crackles and edema, and
> creatinine has gone from 1.0 to 1.6. I think this is expected cardiorenal
> physiology and I want to keep diuresing, but I am not confident. Do not tell
> me what to do. Ask me two questions that would change your mind, then tell me
> what I have missed.
:::

The first prompt gets a plan, and sometimes it will be the plan in the draft
note. The second gets a conversation in which you say what you think first.
That is the arrangement in which being wrong teaches you something. It is also
a better conversation: try it and see.

### Four rules for the wards

- **You sign the note.** Whatever drafted it, the signature and the
  responsibility are yours. *If you could not have written it, do not sign
  it.*
- **Use the covered account.** At CU Anschutz, ChatGPT Edu and Microsoft
  Copilot are covered by a business associate agreement (the contract that
  makes the company responsible for patient data) when you sign in with
  university credentials; a personal account is not. In this course, use made-up cases
  only. See [the patient information page](../course/patient-information.qmd).
- **Document what your institution asks.** Some systems add a line to
  AI-drafted notes; some ask you to attest. [VERIFY: current attestation and
  disclosure language at the course institution; policies differ by system
  and change yearly]{.verify} You should always be able to answer "did a tool
  draft this?" honestly.
- **Read before you send.** When one health system turned on AI-drafted
  replies to patient messages, clinicians used the drafts for about 20% of
  replies. Reply time did not change, but their task load and exhaustion
  scores fell [@pmid:38506805]. That fits clinicians who read and edit the
  drafts, which is the centaur version of the task.

## Do

Use your university ChatGPT Edu or Copilot account, and made-up material only.

### Part A: try it on three tasks (about 35 minutes)

Do all three. For each, try one prompt, then improve it at least once.

**1. Get ready for journal club.** Use the abstract of any paper you have
already read, or of the first trial in this chapter (search PubMed for
"Large Language Model Influence on Diagnostic Reasoning"). Paste the abstract
and try:

```
I am a fourth-year medical student presenting this paper at journal club.
Explain it to me in three levels: one sentence, one paragraph, and the
details a skeptical attending would ask about. Then give me three questions
I should be ready to answer.
```

**2. Make a patient handout.** Pick a common condition in your specialty.
Ask for a one-page handout at a sixth-grade reading level. Then make it
better twice: ask for something specific (shorter, a list of warning signs,
the questions a patient should ask). Check one medical fact in it against a
source you trust.

**3. Learn, do not just get an answer.** Write your own hint-seeking prompt
with Who / Where / What, for the made-up heart-failure patient or a three-line
made-up case of your own. Use the example above as a model, not a copy.
Answer the tool's questions. Then type: "Now quiz me on this. Three
questions, one at a time, and tell me when I am wrong."

Then record the best of the three:

```
The task where the tool helped most: ______________________________

My best prompt (the version I would use again):
__________________________________________________________________

What I changed from my first try, and why it worked better:
__________________________________________________________________

One thing I checked, and whether the tool had it right:
__________________________________________________________________
```

Save that prompt somewhere you will find it in July. It is the first entry in
your own toolkit.

### Part B: sort four tasks (10 minutes)

For each task below, write a verdict (centaur, cyborg, or not at all) and one
sentence of reasoning, using @fig-modes.

```
1. Drafting a progress note          ______  _________________________________
2. Writing a progress note           ______  _________________________________
3. The discharge summary, bed 12     ______  _________________________________
4. The question for nephrology       ______  _________________________________
```

The first two are deliberately a pair. If you gave them the same verdict, ask
what the difference is between a task where you are already writing and one
where nobody is. Most of the learning in this part is in that pair.

## Check

| You have | Meets | Falls short |
|---|---|---|
| Three tasks tried | Each tried at least twice, with one improvement you can describe | One prompt each, no second try |
| A kept prompt | It is specific (who, where, what) and you would use it again | A generic prompt like "explain this paper" |
| One check | A fact checked against a source, and what you found | No check, or "it seemed right" |
| A hint prompt | You wrote it yourself with who, where, and what, and answered the quiz | The example pasted unchanged |
| Four sorted tasks | Each verdict has a reason, and the draft/write pair differs or you say why not | Verdicts without reasons |
| The three perils | You can name one habit that protects against each | "Be careful" |

## What this changes for you

*What does this change about how you'll practice?* Go back to 6:10 a.m. The
senior resident has said "have it draft the notes." Say in two sentences which
lines on the list go to the machine, in which way, and which one does not.
Then add one thing from Part A you will use that she has not thought of.

Then the sentence this course collects and rereads at the end. *Which part of
clinical judgment will you not hand over, and why?* Write it, date it, and
keep it. A task and a reason, not a slogan. If you cannot name one yet, write
that down instead; it is an honest answer.

## Summary

- It is your job to learn where these tools help your work, and you learn it
  by trying. The edge of what they do well is jagged, so nobody can map it
  for you.
- A centaur divides the work and checks it; a cyborg blends the work and goes
  back and forth. The task's risk and the tool's validation decide which.
- In one trial, physicians with a model did no better than without; in a
  second, on a different task, they did better. The task, and how they worked
  with the tool, made the difference.
- Deskilling, never-skilling, and mis-skilling have different defenses. Ask
  for hints, teach back, and get quizzed, and the tool makes you better
  rather than replacing your learning.
- You sign the note. If you could not have written it, do not sign it.

## Go deeper

**Papers**

- The review this chapter is based on, with the three perils, adaptive
  expertise, and DEFT-AI, a five-question debrief for when a supervisor asks
  how you used a tool [@pmid:40834302].
- The two physician trials: diagnosis [@pmid:39466245] and management
  [@pmid:39910272].
- Never-skilling in a randomized field experiment [@pmid:40560616], and
  deskilling in a multicenter observational study [@pmid:40816301].
- The learner study behind five of the six habits [@doi:10.1111/bjet.13544].
- The consultants' experiment that gave centaur, cyborg, and the jagged
  frontier their meaning [@doi:10.2139/ssrn.4573321].
- AI-drafted patient replies at scale: no time saved, burden reduced
  [@pmid:38506805].

**Listen**

- *NEJM AI Grand Rounds*, "AI and the Evolution of Medical Thought with Dr.
  Adam Rodman" (June 19, 2024; 53 min): what clinicians have handed to
  instruments before, and what happened to the skill each time.
  <https://ai-podcast.nejm.org/e/ai-and-the-evolution-of-medical-thought-with-dr-adam-rodman>

**Talks**

- [Prompt engineering](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-10-17-prompt-engineering/):
  ten rules with clinical examples. Who / Where / What is a shortened form of
  the first three. [The prompting lab](enrichment-prompting-lab.qmd) builds on
  this deck.
- [AI in medical education](https://talks.seandavis.net/archive/2024-10-23-ai-in-medical-education/):
  attribution and academic integrity, for when a tool helps with something
  that has your name on it.
